questions.question_text:
A graph is shown below with radian tick labels on the $x$-axis.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.3, xmax=6.8, ymin=-1.4, ymax=1.4,
  xtick={1.5708, 3.1416, 4.7124, 6.2832},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, $2\pi$},
  ytick={-1, 1},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:6.2832] {sin(deg(x))};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Which function does this graph represent on the domain $[0, 2\pi]$?

options.why: Confused with $y = \cos x$, which starts at $(0,1)$ rather than $(0,0)$.
Confused with $y = \tan x$, which has vertical asymptotes.
The graph starts by rising into positive values, so it is $+\sin x$, not $-\sin x$.

questions.solution_text: The curve starts at $(0,0)$, peaks at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$, and returns to $0$ at $\pi$ and $2\pi$. This is $y = \sin x$.

questions.question_text: What are the period and amplitude of the function $y = \cos x$ in radians?

options.why: Used the period of the tangent function ($\pi$) instead of cosine ($2\pi$).
Confused the full range width ($2$) with the amplitude ($1$).
Stated the period in degrees rather than radians.

questions.solution_text: $y = \cos x$ oscillates between $-1$ and $1$ (amplitude $1$) and repeats every $2\pi\text{ radians}$ (period $2\pi$).

questions.question_text:
A graph of the function $y = 2\cos x$ is shown below on the domain $[0, 2\pi]$.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$},
  xmin=-0.3, xmax=6.8, ymin=-2.6, ymax=2.6,
  xtick={1.5708, 3.1416, 4.7124, 6.2832},
  xticklabels={$\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, $2\pi$},
  ytick={-2, -1, 1, 2},
  samples=200, clip=false,
  axis line style={-{Stealth}}, width=11cm, height=6.5cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, blue, domain=0:6.2832] {2*cos(deg(x))};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
What are the coordinates of the minimum turning point of the graph?

options.why: Used the minimum value of standard $y = \cos x$ ($-1$) without accounting for the amplitude of $2$.
Used the $x$-coordinate where $y = \sin x$ reaches its minimum ($x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$) instead of cosine ($x = \pi$).
Identified an $x$-intercept instead of the minimum turning point.

questions.solution_text:
The minimum value of $\cos x$ is $-1$, which occurs at $x = \pi$.
$y = 2\cos\pi$
$=2(-1)$
$=-2$
Therefore, the coordinates of the minimum turning point are $(\pi, -2)$.

options.why: Identified the $x$-intercepts of the tangent graph rather than the vertical asymptotes.
Gave the vertical asymptotes in the domain $[0, 2\pi]$ instead of $[-\pi, \pi]$.
Selected points where $\tan x = \pm 1$, which are regular points on the curve rather than asymptotes.

questions.solution_text:
Vertical asymptotes of $y = \tan x$ occur where $\cos x = 0$.
In the domain $[-\pi, \pi]$, $\cos x = 0$ at $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the symmetry and parity of $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$?

options.text: $y = \sin x$ is odd (origin symmetry); $y = \cos x$ is even ($y$-axis reflection symmetry).
$y = \sin x$ is even ($y$-axis symmetry); $y = \cos x$ is odd (origin symmetry).
options.why: Swapped the parities of the sine and cosine functions.

options.text: Both $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$ are even functions.
options.why: Incorrectly claimed sine is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

options.text: Both $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$ are odd functions.
options.why: Incorrectly claimed cosine has point symmetry about the origin.

questions.solution_text:
$\sin(-x) = -\sin x$ (odd, rotational symmetry about origin).
$\cos(-x) = \cos x$ (even, reflection symmetry about $y$-axis).

questions.question_text: How many solutions does the equation $\sin x = 0.8$ have in the domain $0 \le x \le 2\pi$?

options.why: Only counted the first-quadrant solution, missing the second-quadrant solution.
Double-counted across two periods rather than the single period $[0, 2\pi]$.
Assumed $0.8$ lies outside the range $[-1, 1]$.

questions.solution_text: The horizontal line $y = 0.8$ intersects the sine wave twice in $[0, 2\pi]$: once in Quadrant $1$ and once in Quadrant $2$.

questions.question_text: What are the domain and range of the function $y = \sin x$ for all real $x$ in interval notation?

options.why: Restricted the domain to one cycle rather than all real numbers.
Gave the range of tangent instead of sine.
Swapped domain and range.

questions.solution_text: Sine is defined for all real $x$ (domain $(-\infty, \infty)$) and oscillates between $-1$ and $1$ (range $[-1, 1]$).

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = \tan x$ has period $\pi$.
If $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}$, what is the value of $\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ by periodicity?

options.why: Changed the sign when adding a full period $\pi$.
Confused with $\tan\frac{\pi}{6}$.
Thought $\frac{4\pi}{3}$ is an asymptote of tangent.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \pi$
Since the tangent function has period $\pi$, $\tan\left(x + \pi\right) = \tan x$.
$\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}$

questions.question_text: Find all solutions to the equation $\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the domain $[0, 2\pi]$.

options.why: These are solutions to $\cos x = +\frac{1}{2}$, not $-\frac{1}{2}$.
These are solutions to $\cos x = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
These are solutions to $\cos x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

questions.solution_text:
$\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ occurs in Quadrants $2$ and $3$.
Reference angle: $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$
Quadrant $2$: $x = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$
Quadrant $3$: $x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
